READING PASSAGE 1
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1
on pages 2 and 3.
The development of art appreciation in
Melbourne, Australia
In the 1850s the British colony of Victoria in Australia was growing very quickly as more
people came to live there. In general, the fine arts were not considered to be important at
this time. This was partly because there was a gold rush that was catching people’s
attention far more as it was bringing wealth to the people of Victoria. However, by the
late 1850s, enthusiasm for the fine arts and for a public art museum was beginning to
strengthen. In the city of Melbourne established artists, such as Thomas Clark and
Nicholas Chevalier, were trying to make a living from their art and journalists like
James Smith were becoming known as cultural critics. When the Melbourne Public
Library opened in 1856, it was always expected that the library would eventually house
a public art museum. Frederick McCoy, professor of natural science at the University of
Melbourne, promoted the idea when he suggested placing a museum, focused on the
education of citizens about art, on the ground floor of the Public Library. From the
beginning, there were opposing views about the public art museum’s role. Some people
thought that the most effective way to educate people in art appreciation would be
through demonstrating the history and development of art over the centuries whereas
others felt that it would be better to display original paintings.
In 1858, the Public Library trustees applied to the government for land at the rear of the
library with the intention of building a museum of art. The application was approved
and when the trustees decided that original art works would be too expensive, precise
instructions were given for the purchase of a number of good quality reproductions of
paintings and sculptures. It was felt that this would be the best way to illustrate the
history of art and culture, and provide diverse examples from which local artists and
artisans could learn. Learning about classical art in a museum of art was considered to
be a transformative experience in art appreciation for individuals and society as a whole.
The Museum of Art was opened to the public on 24 May 1861. The Sculpture Gallery,
although crammed into a limited space in the Museum of Art, revealed the Museum’s
desire for the exhibits to have an educational role. Instead of genuine sculptures, casts
reproducing sculptures were obtained and grouped chronologically, that is beginning
with examples from ancient times and working through the eras to contemporary
exhibits, in order to illustrate the historical development of art. Visitors to the Museum
of Art learned about individual works by reading the written information on cards
accompanying each object.
Enthusiasm grew for a new picture gallery; this was partly as a result of the 1861
Victoria Exhibition in Melbourne and the 1862 London Exhibition Cr International
Exhibition) which, in their displays, gave greater recognition to local artists. This
resulted in a greater public interest in art exhibitions and in 1863 the government of
Victoria gave one thousand pounds for the creation of a public picture gallery which was
to display examples of contemporary art. This new public picture gallery soon became
known as the National Gallery and was free to visit. In order to maximise the number of

visitors, it was open in the evenings. Since the art collection was considered to be public
property, it was decided that the public’s care and attention would safeguard it from
theft and damage. To address concerns that the pictures were only available to the
people of Melbourne, the Commission planned to circulate the improving and elevating
influences of art throughout Victoria by lending works for exhibition in country towns.
From October 1866 to February 1867, an Intercolonial Exhibition was held in a
temporary exhibition building erected in the library’s grounds. The picture collection was
moved from the National Gallery for the duration of the exhibition. Almost half the total
population of Victoria visited the exhibition. Such a large display of art works, mostly by
Australian artists, broadened public interest in art produced in Australia. The publicity
given to their work encouraged local artists, and the opportunity to compare and
evaluate the works of local artists enhanced art criticism.
After consideration, the role of the public art museum in Victoria was given a clearer
definition and in 1870 changes were made that reflected the acceptance of a new attitude
to art. The Museum of Art’s educational casts of sculptures were no longer on display but
instead were relegated to the National Gallery’s new Schools of Design and Painting for
instructing art students. Art works that were valued for their educational purpose,
rather than solely their visual appeal, were placed in a separate study room. No longer
encouraging public taste and knowledge through classical art, the National Gallery
would value original paintings and encourage a love of art through the display of
exhibits that reflected the art people liked and valued.

Questions 1-6
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 1-6 on your answer sheet, write
TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this
1 The lack of interest in the fine arts in Victoria in the 1850s was due to a gold rush
taking place.
2 Victoria was the poorest area of Australia before the gold rush.
3 There was disagreement on the purpose of the public art museum in the Melbourne
Public Library.
4 Sculpture casts in the Museum of Art were arranged according to where they came
from.
5 The Intercolonial Exhibition was housed in a pre-existing permanent exhibition centre
in Melbourne.
6 Critical comment on Australian art was improved by the Intercolonial Exhibition.
